title: The Udāna
altTitles: The Solemn Utterances of the Buddha
dateDisplay: Verses c. 3rd–2nd century BCE; commentary c. 5th century CE
attributionNote: The Udāna is a canonical collection without an author. Its eighty discourses are ascribed to the Buddha and were assembled by the early Buddhist community; the verse at the end of each discourse is the udāna, the solemn utterance that gives the book its name.
description: The Udāna gathers eighty short discourses in eight chapters, each closing with a verse the Buddha is said to have spoken on that occasion. The subjects are the whole range of the early teaching: the chain of dependent origination under the Bodhi tree, the monk who cannot be shaken by Māra, the leper Suppabuddha, the quarrelsome monks of Kosambī, the blind men and the elephant, and the Buddha's refusal to name a successor. It is one of the most quoted books of the Pali canon, and its stories are among the oldest surviving Buddhist narratives.
historicalContext: The Udāna belongs to the Khuddaka Nikāya, the miscellaneous collection of the Pali canon, and its oldest verses go back to the oral period. Major-General G. M. Strong's translation, published in London in 1902, was the first complete English Udāna and remains the version the archive carries, with the translator's notes on Pali terms and on the commentarial tradition.
availabilityNote: Complete. All eight chapters and eighty discourses of Strong's translation are streamed from the Internet Sacred Text Archive at read time, one chapter (vagga) per chapter. The volume's title page, preface and introduction are not part of the work; the footnotes printed on each page are kept.
